title: Writing practice: Surveys, areas, food chains, and ancient Rome
description: Eight writing tasks: use survey data, explain an area, trace a food chain, argue about Roman engineering, and write an email to the librarian.

stimuli.title: How we learn new words
stimuli.caption: Mr. Lee's class has 24 students. Each student chose the one activity that helps them learn new words best.

stimuli.title: The garden and the pond
paragraphs: A rectangular garden is 8 meters long and 5 meters wide. In the middle of the garden there is a square pond. Each side of the pond is 2 meters long. Plants cannot grow in the pond.
Picture the garden as a large rectangle with a small square cut out of the middle.

stimuli.title: Changes in an ocean community
stimuli.caption: A cloudy, rainy spring reduced the sunlight reaching the ocean near a coast. The table compares Year 1 (a sunny spring) with Year 2 (a cloudy spring). Phytoplankton are tiny living things that make their own food using sunlight. Krill, which are small shrimp-like animals, eat phytoplankton. Small fish eat krill, and seals eat small fish.

stimuli.title: Read: Roads and Aqueducts in Ancient Rome
paragraphs: Ancient Rome grew from a small city into a large empire that stretched around the Mediterranean Sea. Roman engineers built two kinds of structures that helped the empire work.

The first was a network of paved roads. Roads allowed soldiers to march to distant places, and they let merchants carry goods such as olive oil and grain from one region to another. Messengers also used the roads to deliver official letters.

The second was the aqueduct, a channel that carried fresh water from springs and rivers to cities. Aqueducts were built with a gentle downward slope so that water could flow by gravity. The water supplied public fountains and baths, and it helped large cities stay healthy and clean.
People can disagree about which structure mattered more to Rome's success.

stimuli.title: A message to the librarian
paragraphs: You are working on a science project about volcanoes, and it is due on Friday. You looked on the library shelf for a long time, but you could not find a book that explains how volcanoes erupt. The library closes at 4:00 today. The school librarian, Mr. Ibrahim, can help students find books.

stimuli.title: Read: How Ants Share Directions
paragraphs: When a worker ant finds food, such as a crumb or a dead insect, it returns to the nest. On the way back, it touches the ground with the tip of its body and leaves a thin trail of a chemical scent. People cannot smell this trail, but other ants can sense it with their antennae.

Other ants follow the scent trail to the food. Each ant that finds the food and walks back to the nest adds more scent to the trail. A trail with more scent attracts more ants, so a good food source soon has a long line of ants carrying food. When the food runs out, ants stop adding scent. The scent slowly fades, and the ants stop coming.

Scientists have shown this with simple experiments. When they wiped part of a trail away, the ants became confused and wandered in different directions until they found the trail again. Because of scent trails, hundreds of ants in a colony can find the same food without any ant giving directions.

stimuli.title: Lina's multiplication examples
stimuli.caption: Lina tried four multiplications with numbers greater than 0 and wrote the answers.

stimuli.title: Three kinds of rock
stimuli.caption: A fact sheet for a science display.
rows: Small pieces of rock and shell settle in layers and are pressed together
Heat and pressure change an existing rock

items.stem: Write a claim about which activity helps the most students in this class learn new words. Support your claim with numbers from the table. Then give one reason you think the activity works.

checklist: I made a clear claim.
I used at least two numbers from the table.
I gave a reason in my own words.
I used a connecting word such as because or however.
exemplar: Claim identifies word games as the choice of the most students
Evidence includes accurate numbers (11 of 24, compared with 9 and 4)
Reasoning links the evidence to the claim and adds a personal or logical reason
Uses comparison language (more than, the most, fewer)
Writes complete sentences joined with connectors

support.clue: Look at which row has the biggest number. Then compare it with the other two numbers. Think about why that activity could help you remember words.
support.frame: I claim that ______ helps the most students learn new words. The table shows that ______ students chose it, but only ______ chose ______. This shows that ______. I think it works because ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different survey. “I claim that walking is the most popular way to get to school. The table shows that 14 students walk, but only 6 ride the bus. This shows that most of the class lives close to the school. I think it is popular because it is free and easy.” Notice the claim, the numbers, and the reason. Write about learning words the same way.

facts: 9 + 11 + 4 = 24 students, which matches the class size given in the caption.

items.stem: Explain how to find the area of the garden where plants can grow. Show each step.

checklist: I explained how to find the area of the whole garden.
I explained how to find the area of the pond.
I used math words such as multiply or subtract, and I gave the final answer with units.
I used order words such as first, next, and then.
exemplar: Finds the area of the whole garden correctly: 8 × 5 = 40 square meters
Finds the area of the pond correctly: 2 × 2 = 4 square meters
Subtracts to find the planting area: 36 square meters, with units
Explains the steps in order and says why subtraction is needed (the pond cannot be planted)

support.clue: Think about what part of the garden you can plant in. What do you need to find first?
support.frame: First, I found the area of ______ by ______, which is ______ square meters. Next, I ______. Then I ______. The planting area is ______ because ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different shape. “A hallway is made of two rectangles joined together. The first part is 6 meters by 3 meters, and the second part is 2 meters by 3 meters. First, I find the area of the first part: 6 × 3 = 18 square meters. Next, I find the area of the second part: 2 × 3 = 6 square meters. Then I add the two areas because both parts need new floor. The hallway floor is 24 square meters.” Notice that each step says what the numbers mean. Explain the garden the same way.

facts: The area of a rectangle is length times width.
8 × 5 = 40 square meters; 2 × 2 = 4 square meters; 40 − 4 = 36 square meters.

items.stem: Write an explanation of how less sunlight in Year 2 affected the living things in the ocean. Follow the chain from sunlight to seals, use data from the table, and explain why each change happened.

checklist: I started with the effect of less sunlight on phytoplankton.
I followed the chain: phytoplankton, krill, small fish, seals.
I used numbers from the table for at least three living things.
I explained why each change caused the next change.
I used sequence words and cause-and-effect words.
exemplar: Begins with the cause: less sunlight means phytoplankton make less food and the amount of phytoplankton falls from 100 to 60 units
Follows the chain in order: fewer phytoplankton, less food for krill (100 to 72), less food for small fish (100 to 85), fewer seals (12 to 10)
Explains the feeding relationships that link each change to the next
Uses precise science vocabulary and varied causal connectors
Uses the data accurately

support.clue: Start with the sunlight and the phytoplankton row. Then move down the table one row at a time and ask: what does this living thing eat, and what happened to that food?
support.frame: Because there was less sunlight in Year 2, ______. As a result, the amount of phytoplankton ______ from ______ to ______. Krill eat ______, so ______. This led to ______. Since small fish eat ______, ______. Finally, ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different chain of events. “When a storm knocked down power lines, the traffic lights stopped working. As a result, cars moved more slowly through the crossroads. Because of this, the buses were late. Finally, many students arrived at school after the bell.” Notice how each event leads to the next one. Explain the ocean community the same way.

facts: Phytoplankton use sunlight to make food (photosynthesis).
In a food chain, a decrease in the amount of food can lead to a decrease in the living things that eat it.
Krill eat phytoplankton, small fish eat krill, and seals eat small fish (stated in the stimulus).
The numbers in the table are invented data.

items.stem: Which mattered more to the growth of the Roman Empire: roads or aqueducts? Write an argument that states your position, uses at least two pieces of evidence from the passage, and explains your reasoning.

checklist: I chose roads or aqueducts and said why it mattered more.
I used two details from the passage as evidence.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
I wrote about the other structure and explained why it mattered less.
I used connectors such as because, although, and therefore.
exemplar: States a clear position about which structure mattered more
Uses evidence from the passage (soldiers, merchants, and messengers on roads, or fresh water for large cities)
Reasoning connects the evidence to the growth of the empire (control, trade, health, population)
Addresses the other structure with concession or rebuttal language
Uses historical vocabulary (empire, merchants, engineers) and a claim, evidence, reasoning organization

support.clue: Make a two-column list from the passage: what roads did, and what aqueducts did. Then decide which list shows more about how the empire grew and stayed together.
support.frame: I believe that ______ mattered more to the Roman Empire because ______. According to the passage, ______. This shows that ______. Although ______ also ______, ______. Therefore, ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different pair. “I believe that the microphone mattered more to the school play than the curtain because the audience could hear every word. According to the program notes, 300 people filled the hall. This shows that many people were sitting far from the stage. Although the curtain helped the actors change scenes, the play still works without it. Therefore, the microphone was more important.” Notice the position, the evidence from a source, the reasoning, and the answer to the other side. Do the same with roads and aqueducts.

facts: Ancient Rome became an empire that surrounded the Mediterranean Sea.
Roman roads were paved routes used by soldiers, merchants, and messengers.
Roman aqueducts carried fresh water to cities, using a gentle downward slope so that water flowed by gravity.

items.stem: Write an email to Mr. Ibrahim. Explain what you need and why you need it, and ask him politely for help.

checklist: I used a greeting such as Dear Mr. Ibrahim.
I explained what I need and why.
I used because or so to give a reason.
I asked politely for help and ended politely.
exemplar: Uses an appropriate email format with a greeting, body, and closing
Explains the need and the reason with cause-and-effect language (the project is due Friday, the book was not on the shelf)
Makes a clear, polite request for help
Uses a polite, respectful register for a school adult (please, could you, thank you)
Presents ideas in a clear, logical order

support.clue: Think about three parts: what you need, why you need it, and what you want Mr. Ibrahim to do. Use the information about the project in the scenario.
support.frame: Dear Mr. Ibrahim, I am looking for a book about ______ because ______. I looked ______, but ______. Could you please ______? Thank you, ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different message. “Dear Ms. Park, I need a ruler for my art project because mine broke this morning. I looked in my backpack, but I could not find another one. Could you please lend me a ruler for today? Thank you, Lena.” Notice the greeting, the reason with because, a polite request, and a closing. Write your email the same way.

items.stem: Write an informational paragraph for a science magazine for younger students. Explain what an ant scent trail is and what it helps the colony do, using your own words.

checklist: I wrote a topic sentence that tells the main idea.
I explained at least two things about how the trail works.
I used my own words instead of copying sentences.
I wrote a closing sentence that shows why the trail is useful.
exemplar: Topic sentence identifies the scent trail as a way ants share where food is
Accurate details: an ant leaves scent on the way back to the nest, other ants follow it with their antennae, and more ants add more scent
Paraphrases the source with synonyms and varied sentence structures
Explains vocabulary for a younger audience
Closing sentence states the usefulness of the trail to the colony

support.clue: Find the sentence that says what the scent trail is for. Then find how other ants follow it and what happens as more ants use the trail.
support.frame: An ant scent trail is ______ that ants use to ______. One thing ants do is ______. Other ants ______. Over time, ______. As a result, ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different animal. “The beaver's tail slap is a signal that warns other beavers of danger. One thing the slap shows is that a threat is near. It does this by making a loud sound on the water. As a result, nearby beavers dive into the water and hide.” Notice the main idea first, then details in the writer's own words. Write about the waggle dance the same way.

facts: Many ants leave a chemical scent trail when they carry food back to the nest.
Other ants sense the scent with their antennae and follow the trail to the food.
When the food is gone, ants stop adding scent and the trail fades.
Beavers slap their tails on the water to warn other beavers of danger.

items.stem: Lina says, “When you multiply a number by another number, the product is always larger than the number you started with.” Decide whether her claim is always true. Write an argument that explains why her four examples are not enough, gives one example of your own with exact numbers, and says what is true instead.

checklist: I said whether Lina's claim is always true.
I explained why four examples that fit are not enough to prove it.
I gave my own example with exact numbers and showed the calculation.
I explained what is true instead.
I used mathematical language and connectors such as however and therefore.
exemplar: Takes a clear position that the claim is not always true
Explains that examples that fit do not prove a general claim, but one counterexample can disprove it
Gives an accurate counterexample, such as 8 × 0.5 = 4, 12 × 1/4 = 3, or 9 × 1 = 9
Explains the reasoning: multiplying by a number less than 1 takes only part of the starting number
Corrects the claim accurately and uses precise vocabulary (product, factor, counterexample)

support.clue: Look at the second numbers in the four examples. What kinds of numbers has Lina not tried?
support.frame: I disagree with Lina's claim because ______. Her examples all ______, but one example that does not fit is ______ × ______ = ______. This shows that ______. In fact, when you multiply by a number ______, the product ______ because ______. A more accurate claim is ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different claim. “I disagree with Omar’s claim that all birds can fly. His examples are a sparrow, an eagle, a robin, and a duck, but one example that does not fit is the penguin. This shows that the claim is not always true. In fact, some birds, such as penguins and ostriches, cannot fly because their bodies and wings are built for swimming or running. A more accurate claim is that most birds can fly.” Notice the counterexample and the corrected claim. Evaluate Lina’s claim the same way.

facts: For positive numbers, multiplying by a number greater than 1 gives a larger product, multiplying by 1 gives the same number, and multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 gives a smaller product.
Penguins and ostriches are birds that cannot fly.

items.stem: Write an informational paragraph for a science display. Tell how the three kinds of rock form, and give an example of each.

checklist: I wrote a topic sentence about the three kinds of rock.
I told how each kind forms.
I gave an example of each kind.
I used science words such as igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic.
exemplar: Topic sentence names the three kinds of rock
Describes how each kind forms accurately
Gives granite, sandstone, and marble as examples
Uses precise science vocabulary and moves through the kinds in order
Uses present tense and varied sentence beginnings

support.clue: Use the middle column of the table to say how each rock forms. Use the last column for examples. Put one kind of rock in each sentence.
support.frame: There are three kinds of rock. Igneous rock forms when ______. An example is ______. Sedimentary rock forms when ______. For example, ______. Metamorphic rock forms when ______. An example is ______.
support.model: Mentor example about a different topic. “There are three kinds of musical instruments in this band. String instruments make sound when strings vibrate. An example is the violin. Wind instruments make sound when air moves through them. An example is the flute. Percussion instruments make sound when they are hit. An example is the drum.” Notice that each kind gets its own sentences. Write about the rocks the same way.

facts: Igneous rock forms when melted rock cools and hardens; granite is igneous.
Sedimentary rock forms when sediments settle in layers and are pressed together; sandstone is sedimentary.
Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change an existing rock; marble is metamorphic.
